items.title: The Great Storm of October 1987
items.summary: A deep Atlantic depression crossed southern England during the night of 15–16 October 1987, bringing destructive winds to England and northern France. The Met Office counts 18 deaths directly caused by the storm in England. About 15 million trees were blown down, and at the peak 3 million homes and businesses were without electricity. Gusts reached 98 knots at Shoreham-by-Sea and at least 216 km/h on the Normandy coast.

impacts.text: The Met Office counts 18 direct storm deaths in England. This excludes deaths in other countries.

The Forestry Commission estimated 15 million fallen trees, representing 3.9 million cubic metres of timber. It reported 3 million householders and businesses without electricity at the peak of the cuts, and no Southern Region trains running on the morning of 16 October.
Buildings and boats were damaged. Fallen trees blocked transport and broke power lines. Gatwick Airport closed.

history.text: Later forecasts shifted the main threat south. Evening broadcasts emphasised rain and missed the exceptional winds. Michael Fish denied that a hurricane was coming; the Met Office says he meant another Atlantic system.
Emergency authorities received warnings, and the Ministry of Defence was alerted at 0135 UTC on 16 October.

Afterwards, more ocean buoys were deployed to watch the seas south-west of the British Isles, and the Met Office set up the National Severe Weather Warning Service to warn emergency services and the public.

why_interesting.text: The low deepened by 17 hPa in 12 hours as it crossed the Bay of Biscay. The pressure rises behind it were exceptional: 12 hPa in one hour at Hurn, near Bournemouth.
Its track took it from west of Spain to north-west of Brittany by 00 GMT 16 Oct, over Exeter at 02 GMT and to Hull around 05–06 GMT. The most damaging winds lay south and south-east of the track.
It became a key case for the sting jet: air descending from the cloud head near its hooked tip, bringing the damaging winds seen in the dry slot.
Some records were revised. The Met Office later reduced Gorleston's 106 knots to 85 knots because the anemometer cups were bent, leaving Shoreham as the strongest measured gust in England.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 reaches 951 hPa off Brittany at 22 UTC 15 Oct, close to published central-pressure analyses of 952–953 hPa around 00 GMT 16 Oct. Its peak gusts at Shoreham are 40 m/s during 03–04 UTC 16 Oct and at Pointe du Roc 35 m/s during 00–01 UTC 16 Oct, below the station evidence. The largest shortfall is at Pointe du Roc, where the recorder reached 60 m/s, so the actual peak remains uncertain. These differences likely reflect the coarse representation of coastlines, exposed headlands and small wind features; London’s rooftop instrument also differs from a standard surface wind measurement.

scenes.title: Across the Atlantic and into the North Sea

captions.text: A small low forms far west of Spain
Deepening fast over the Bay of Biscay
The centre crosses England; isobars tightest over the south-east
Pressure at Shoreham up 29 hPa in 9 hours as the low leaves
Gusts near 40 m/s sweep the Brittany coast
The worst gusts cross Sussex and Kent: 40 m/s at Shoreham
Gales ease inland; the strongest gusts are over the North Sea
High cloud (white) spreads over northern France and England
Cloud hooks round the north side; darker, drier air reaches the centre
Skies clear over France and south-east England behind the storm
